Authenticating a Socket with the Existing JWT

A connection isn't 'anyone' until it hands over the same JWT it already carries for HTTP requests — then it joins a room or two.

Opening a WebSocket connection, on its own, proves nothing about who's on the other end — there's no Authorization header the way an HTTP request has one. Rather than invent a second, socket-specific way to log in, a connected client just sends the same JWT it already got from Week 4's login endpoint, once, over the socket itself:

// Figure 5.13: a JWT proves who's connected, then joins a room or two (src/config/socket.js, excerpt)
io.on('connection', (socket) => {
  socket.on('authenticate', (token) => {
    try {
      const { sub, role } = verifyToken(token);
      socket.join(`user:${sub}`);
      if (role === 'agent' || role === 'admin') {
        socket.join(`role:${role}`);
      }
    } catch {
      socket.disconnect();
    }
  });
});

verifyToken is the exact same function middleware/authenticate.js calls on every HTTP request (Lesson 4) — this project doesn't gain a second authentication scheme, it reuses the one it already has, just handed over once per socket connection instead of once per request. A verified token puts the socket into a room named after that user's id (user:<id>) — Socket.IO's mechanism for "broadcast to this group," which io.to('user:5').emit(...) (next slide) can later target without knowing which specific connection belongs to user 5. Agents and admins also join a shared role:agent/role:admin room, since some events (like ticket.created) are meant for the whole queue, not one specific person. An invalid or expired token disconnects the socket outright, rather than leaving it connected but silently in no room at all — the same "fail loudly rather than quietly do nothing" instinct as authenticate.js.
